concepts.name: Constitutional Appellate Jurisdiction under Article 132: Constitutional Questions
key_dimensions: Requirement of a substantial question of law as to interpretation of the Constitution
Certificate of fitness granted by the High Court as a prerequisite
Applicability to civil, criminal, AND other proceedings — the tripartite coverage often confused
UPSC trap: Article 132 is the ONLY appellate provision that cuts across all three categories (civil/criminal/other) on constitutional grounds

concepts.name: Civil Appellate Jurisdiction under Article 133: Conditions and Limitations
key_dimensions: Requirement of HC certificate that the case involves a substantial question of law of general importance
HC must certify that the question 'needs to be decided' by the Supreme Court — dual threshold
Amendment by the 30th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1972: removal of the valuation criterion
UPSC trap: Article 133 applies ONLY to civil proceedings from High Courts, not criminal; no appeal as of right without HC certificate

concepts.name: Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction under Article 134: Scope and Automatic vs. Certificate-Based Appeal
key_dimensions: Two routes: automatic appeal (without certificate) vs. certificate-based appeal from HC
Automatic appeal conditions: HC reversed acquittal and sentenced to death; HC withdrawn a case and convicted with death sentence
Certificate route: HC certifies the case is fit for appeal to SC in criminal matters
UPSC trap: SC does NOT automatically hear all death penalty cases — only specific HC-order scenarios trigger automatic jurisdiction under 134(1)(a) and (b)

concepts.name: Parliamentary Power to Extend Appellate Jurisdiction under Articles 133(3) and 134(2)
key_dimensions: Parliament can by law confer further appellate jurisdiction on SC in civil matters (Art. 133(3)) and criminal matters (Art. 134(2))
Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970 as a key example
Distinction between constitutional appellate jurisdiction and Parliament-extended jurisdiction
UPSC trap: This is a legislative expansion of jurisdiction, NOT a constitutional amendment — ordinary law suffices

concepts.name: Certificate of Fitness by High Court: Grant, Refusal, and Implications
key_dimensions: Articles 132, 133, and 134 all use HC certificate as the gateway — but conditions differ for each
HC's refusal of certificate does NOT bar the party from seeking Special Leave under Article 136
SC can itself examine whether the certificate was correctly granted
UPSC trap: Certificate under Art. 132/133/134 is from HC; but SLP under Art. 136 is filed directly before SC — these are parallel, not sequential, tracks

concepts.name: Special Leave Petition (SLP) under Article 136: Nature, Scope, and Limitations
key_dimensions: Discretionary and extraordinary jurisdiction — SC may grant leave in its discretion
Covers any judgment, decree, determination, sentence or order by ANY court or tribunal (except military tribunals/courts-martial)
Not an appeal as of right — SC can refuse SLP without assigning reasons
UPSC trap: Art. 136 is NOT an appellate jurisdiction per se but a discretionary power to grant leave; the actual appeal is heard only after leave is granted

concepts.name: Exclusion of Military Tribunals from Article 136 Jurisdiction
key_dimensions: Article 136(2) expressly excludes courts-martial or tribunals constituted under a law relating to the Armed Forces
Rationale: military discipline and separate judicial framework under Army Act, Navy Act, Air Force Act
Contrast with other tribunals (CAT, NGT, etc.) which are covered under Art. 136
UPSC trap: ALL other tribunals and courts fall under Art. 136 EXCEPT military courts — a precise exclusion that examiners test

concepts.name: 'Substantial Question of Law' as a Threshold Concept across Articles 132 and 133
key_dimensions: Judicial interpretation: a question is 'substantial' if it is not covered by settled law and affects rights of parties
Under Art. 132: must be a substantial question of constitutional interpretation specifically
Under Art. 133: must be a substantial question of law of 'general importance' — broader than Art. 132
UPSC trap: The phrase appears in both articles but with different qualifiers — 'constitutional' vs. 'general importance'

concepts.name: Appellate Jurisdiction vs. Original Jurisdiction vs. Advisory Jurisdiction: Conceptual Demarcation
key_dimensions: Original jurisdiction (Art. 131): disputes between states/Centre — no appeal, first instance
Appellate jurisdiction (Arts. 132–134, 136): reviewing decisions of lower courts
Advisory jurisdiction (Art. 143): President's reference — not adjudicatory
UPSC trap: Writ jurisdiction under Art. 32 is original but not the same as Art. 131; appellate SC sits as a court of error, not a court of first instance

concepts.name: Doctrine of 'Court of Record' and its Relationship with Appellate Powers
key_dimensions: Article 129 declares SC a court of record with power to punish for contempt
Being a court of record underpins the SC's authority to correct its own records even while exercising appellate jurisdiction
Distinction: appellate power corrects lower court errors; court-of-record power preserves SC's own dignity
UPSC trap: Review jurisdiction (Art. 137) is separate from appellate jurisdiction — SC can review its OWN appellate judgments

concepts.name: Review Jurisdiction under Article 137 as a Complement to Appellate Jurisdiction
key_dimensions: SC can review any judgment/order made by it, subject to laws made by Parliament and rules under Art. 145
Grounds for review: error apparent on face of record, discovery of new evidence, any sufficient reason
Review is distinct from appeal — no re-hearing; typically decided in chambers without oral arguments
UPSC trap: Curative petition (evolved in Rupa Ashok Hurra case, 2002) is a further remedy AFTER review is dismissed — not a constitutional provision but judicially evolved

concepts.name: Curative Petition: Judicial Evolution Beyond Constitutional Text
key_dimensions: Not mentioned in the Constitution; evolved by SC in Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002)
Filed after dismissal of review petition; heard by 3 senior-most judges + judges who passed the judgment
Grounds: violation of principles of natural justice or apprehension of bias
UPSC trap: Curative petition is the LAST judicial resort, not a constitutional provision — examiners test whether candidates confuse it with review under Art. 137

concepts.name: Transfer of Cases under Article 139A: Overlap with Appellate Jurisdiction
key_dimensions: SC can transfer cases involving the same/substantially same questions of law pending before HC and SC or between two or more HCs
Suo motu transfer vs. party-initiated transfer
Distinction: transfer consolidates cases for uniform ruling; appellate jurisdiction is invoked post-decision by lower court
UPSC trap: Art. 139A was inserted by 44th Amendment, 1978 — not an original provision; often confused with Art. 136 SLP power

concepts.name: Appellate Jurisdiction over Tribunals: Constitutional Amendments and Judicial Pronouncements
key_dimensions: L. Chandra Kumar case (1997): SC held that judicial review by SC/HC is a basic structure feature — tribunal orders must be subject to HC scrutiny first
Rojer Mathew v. South Indian Bank (2019): reaffirmed need for HC jurisdiction as intermediate appellate forum before SC
Parliament cannot oust SC's appellate/supervisory jurisdiction over tribunals via ordinary law

UPSC trap: Though Art. 136 covers tribunals, Parliament's attempt to make SC the FIRST appellate court (bypassing HC) was struck down — judicial review of tribunal orders must go through HC under Art. 226/227 first

concepts.name: Appellate Jurisdiction and the 'Judgment, Decree, Determination, Sentence, or Order' Spectrum under Art. 136
key_dimensions: Art. 136 covers interlocutory orders, not just final judgments — wide textual coverage
SC has held that interim orders causing irreversible harm can be challenged via SLP
Contrast with Arts. 132–134 which are limited to final orders/judgments of HC
UPSC trap: Under Art. 136, even an interlocutory order is challengeable; under Arts. 132–134, the appeal is against a definitive judgment/order — examiners test this textual difference

concepts.name: The 'As of Right' vs. Discretionary Appeal Distinction in SC's Appellate Jurisdiction
key_dimensions: 'As of right' appeals: death sentence reversal under Art. 134(1)(a)/(b) — no certificate needed
Certificate-based appeals under Arts. 132, 133, 134(1)(c): HC must certify fitness
Discretionary appeals under Art. 136: SC decides whether to grant leave
UPSC trap: Very few situations give an automatic right of appeal to SC — examiners probe candidates on which provision grants appeal 'as of right' vs. discretionary leave

concepts.name: High Court as the Feeder Court for SC Appellate Jurisdiction: Role of Articles 132–134
key_dimensions: Arts. 132–134 explicitly refer to appeals from 'High Courts' — not subordinate courts directly
Contrast with Art. 136 (SLP) which covers ANY court or tribunal in India
Hierarchical design: District Court → HC → SC under Arts. 132–134; Art. 136 creates a bypass for extraordinary situations
UPSC trap: SC cannot be approached directly under Arts. 132–134 bypassing HC — these are strictly HC-to-SC appellate tracks

concepts.name: Interaction between Appellate Jurisdiction and Writ Jurisdiction (Art. 32 vs. Art. 136)
key_dimensions: Art. 32 is original jurisdiction for enforcement of fundamental rights — not appellate
A party can simultaneously challenge an HC decision via SLP (Art. 136) and file a fresh writ under Art. 32 only if a distinct FRs violation exists
SC has discouraged invoking Art. 32 when an effective appellate remedy under Art. 136 exists
UPSC trap: Art. 32 cannot be used as a substitute for an appeal — SC has held this in multiple cases; examiners test whether candidates distinguish between the two jurisdictions

concepts.name: Scope of SC's Power to Pass Any Order in Appellate Jurisdiction under Article 142
key_dimensions: Art. 142 empowers SC to pass any order necessary to do complete justice — even while exercising appellate jurisdiction
Used to mould reliefs beyond what the parties prayed for in appellate proceedings
Judicial controversy: Art. 142 cannot override substantive statutory law (Union Carbide case vs. critics)
UPSC trap: Art. 142 is a supplementary power that enhances appellate jurisdiction but is NOT itself appellate jurisdiction — examiners test whether candidates conflate the two

concepts.name: Precedent and Binding Nature of SC Appellate Decisions under Article 141
key_dimensions: Art. 141: law declared by SC is binding on all courts in India
Appellate judgments of SC form binding precedents — even a single-judge SC bench decision binds HCs
Obiter dicta vs. ratio decidendi in appellate judgments: only ratio is binding under Art. 141
UPSC trap: Art. 141 says 'all courts' — this includes HCs and subordinate courts but NOT the SC itself (SC can depart from its own precedent via a larger bench)
